notes: Slot 7 (RCC) fixed and not written. Royal-era establishment split: CYDEF (0), royal-era cabinet men (1), Bakkush reformers (2), Shalhi clan (15), Sa'adi tribes (14), Senussi order (10), House of Senussi (23). No Libyan Shia: slot 8 holds the Ibadi Amazigh of Jabal Nafusa, slot 9 a small Iraqi/Lebanese Shia expatriate circle. Arab Nationalist Movement in 18 (popularity), Ba'ath in 6, Italian settler nostalgics in 21.

0.name: Quwwat Difa' Barqa
0.text:
The Cyrenaica Defence Force was King Idris's praetorian gendarmerie, recruited from loyal Cyrenaican tribes, armed with British equipment and deliberately kept stronger than the regular army. On 1 September 1969 it failed to resist the Free Officers, and since then its units have been disarmed, merged into the army and purged of royalist commanders.

Its surviving officers look to the exiled court and to London and Washington, hoping that the British at El Adem and the Americans at Wheelus will not abandon the old order. Their programme is restoration of the monarchy, close alliance with the West and tribal autonomy in the east, and their leverage lies in eastern tribal networks and arms caches.

1.name: Rijal al-Ahd al-Malaki
1.text:
The Men of the Royal Era are the prime ministers, ministers and senators who governed the United Kingdom of Libya until September 1969. Figures such as Mahmud al-Muntasir, Hussein Maziq and the last premier Wanis al-Qaddafi are now detained by the revolutionary regime and await prosecution, while others have slipped abroad.

They stand for a constitutional monarchy, the federal traditions of Tripolitania, Cyrenaica and Fezzan, cautious development financed by oil and close ties with Britain, the United States and conservative Arab states. Their base is the old notability, senior civil servants and families enriched under the crown; their influence survives in patronage networks the new officers have not yet dismantled.

2.name: Al-Shakhsiyya al-Libiyya
2.text:
The Libyan Personality is the reformist circle around Abd al-Hamid al-Bakkush, the young lawyer who served as prime minister in 1967-68 and promoted a modern, self-confident Libyan national identity distinct from Nasser's pan-Arabism. Dismissed by the court for being too ambitious, Bakkush has been detained by the Revolutionary Command Council since the coup.

His followers among university graduates, lawyers and modern-minded officials want a constitutional state, rule of law, an efficient administration and oil revenues spent on education. They favour cooperation with the West without subservience and distrust both the old court and the officers. Their strength is intellectual credibility among the educated middle class rather than any organized machine.

3.name: Al-Ittihad al-Amm li-Ummal Libya
3.text:
The Libyan General Workers' Union grew out of the Tripoli labour movement of the 1950s under Salem Shita and became the main federation of port, construction and oil workers. Under the monarchy it alternated between bargaining with the government and politically charged strikes; since September 1969 the revolutionary officers have courted it while preparing to bring it under state control.

Its leaders favour collective bargaining, higher wages from oil wealth, Libyanization of foreign company jobs and a measure of union independence. Tied historically to Western labour internationals yet increasingly drawn to Arab socialism, it draws strength from the oilfields, the ports of Tripoli and Benghazi and the growing urban workforce.

4.name: Al-Tali'a al-Hamra
4.text:
The Red Vanguard is the loose network of clandestine Marxist-Leninist cells among oil workers at Brega and Ras Lanuf, students in Benghazi and Tripoli and Arab teachers recruited from Sudan, Iraq and Egypt. Libya has never had a legal communist party, and these circles survive by reading groups and contacts with the Sudanese and Iraqi communist parties.

They welcome the fall of the monarchy and the expulsion of the British and American bases, and urge the officers to nationalize oil and seek Soviet friendship. Yet they reject the officers' Islamic puritanism and ban on parties. Their influence is small but concentrated in the oil sector and the university.

5.name: Al-Ittihad al-Amm li-Talabat Libya
5.text:
The General Union of Libyan Students is the student body of the University of Libya in Benghazi and Tripoli and of Libyan students abroad. Its militants led the January 1964 demonstrations against the monarchy and the foreign bases, when police fire killed students in Benghazi, and it greeted the September revolution with enthusiasm.

Nasserists, Ba'athists, Marxists and independent radicals compete inside it, demanding rapid evacuation of the bases, an end to corruption, free speech and real power for the young generation. Its leverage is mobilization in the streets and the campuses; the officers already sense that a politically independent student movement could become a rival.

6.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki
6.english: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party – Libya Region
6.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr Libya
6.text:
The Libyan region of the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party took root in the 1950s among students, teachers and lawyers returning from Damascus, Baghdad and Cairo. The monarchy prosecuted its leaders in 1961, and since the September revolution the party remains illegal, tolerated only as individuals while the officers insist on a single Nasserist-style organization.

Its members preach unity, freedom and socialism, uncompromising hostility to Western bases and oil companies, and alignment with the Arab revolutionary camp. Divided between sympathies for Damascus and Baghdad, they distrust Gaddafi's personal rule. Their weight lies in the intelligentsia, the teaching profession and contacts inside the civil service.

8.name: Warathat al-Baruni
8.text:
The Heirs of al-Baruni are the Ibadi Amazigh notables, teachers and merchants of Jabal Nafusa and Zuwara who invoke Sulayman al-Baruni, the Ibadi scholar and leader of the 1918 Tripolitanian Republic. Libya's only non-Sunni Muslim community, they are loyal but uneasy under a revolution that exalts Arab identity.

They seek recognition of Ibadi religious schools and of the Amazigh language, modern education for the mountain villages and fair access to state jobs. Theologically moderate and reformist, they prefer quiet negotiation to confrontation. Their leverage lies in a cohesive community, commercial networks reaching Tunisia and Algeria, and a reputation for integrity in trade.

9.name: Jama'at al-Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a small group of Shia teachers, doctors and engineers from Iraq and southern Lebanon recruited by Libya's expanding schools and hospitals. They follow the Najaf seminaries and the marja' Muhsin al-Hakim, and some are touched by the clandestine Islamic Da'wa ideas spreading among young Iraqi Shia.

They hold that legitimate rule belongs to men of religious learning and condemn both the secular Ba'ath in Baghdad and Western influence. In Libya they keep a low profile, meeting in private homes. Their only leverage is their professional standing and the links they could open between Tripoli and the Shia world.

10.name: Al-Tariqa al-Sanusiyya
10.text:
The Senussi Order is the Sufi brotherhood founded in 1837 by Muhammad bin Ali al-Senussi, whose network of zawiyas organized the tribes of Cyrenaica, led resistance against Italy and gave Libya its royal house. Since the coup its lodges and the Islamic University at al-Bayda are under suspicion, and its properties are being taken over by the state.

The order stands for a reformist yet orthodox Islam, the authority of the brotherhood's shaykhs, the sanctity of the monarchy and social conservatism. It is quietist and pro-Western by default rather than conviction. Its strength lies in Cyrenaican villages, desert oases such as Kufra and Jaghbub, and deep tribal loyalty.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir al-Islami
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, has had clandestine cells in Libya since the 1950s, mostly among students, teachers and junior officials in Tripoli and Benghazi. It rejects both the deposed monarchy and the new republic as illegitimate.

The party seeks the restoration of a single caliphate ruling by Islamic law over all Muslims, regards nationalism and socialism as imported ideologies and condemns Western and Soviet influence alike. It recruits through study circles and pamphlets and hopes to win officers to seize power on its behalf. Its leverage is ideological discipline rather than numbers.

12.name: Al-Ikhwan al-Muslimun fi Libya
12.text:
The Muslim Brotherhood in Libya was planted in 1949 by Egyptian Brothers who fled to Benghazi and were sheltered by Emir Idris. It grew among students, teachers and merchants, but never became a mass party under the monarchy's ban on parties. Since September 1969 it watches the revolutionary officers warily, its members tolerated as individuals.

The Brotherhood calls for a state guided by Islamic law, moral renewal, charitable work and Arab solidarity, and rejects both Western influence and atheistic communism. It distrusts Gaddafi's Nasserist sympathies. Its strength lies in mosques, schools and professional networks in Benghazi and Tripoli, and in ties to Brothers across the Arab world.

13.name: Al-Mu'assasa al-Libiyya al-Amma li-l-Bitrul
13.text:
The Libyan General Petroleum Corporation, created in 1968 to give the state its own stake in the oil industry, has become the home of a new class of Libyan geologists, economists and lawyers. Since the revolution its technocrats work closely with the officers who want a larger share of the revenues from Esso, Oasis and Occidental.

The corporation favours higher posted prices, state participation in concessions and the training of Libyans to replace foreign staff, using oil as leverage without choosing between the blocs. Its power lies in controlling the country's sole source of wealth; whoever commands its expertise holds the key to Libya's budget.

14.name: Qaba'il al-Sa'adi
14.text:
The Sa'adi Tribes are the noble Bedouin tribes of Cyrenaica, among them the Obeidat, Bara'asa, Awaqir and Hasa, whose shaykhs formed the backbone of the Senussi state and of the resistance against Italy. Since the coup they have lost their privileged access to the court and many of their sons in the security forces have been sidelined.

The tribal notables want local autonomy, respect for customary law, land rights on the Jabal al-Akhdar and a fair share of oil revenues for the east. They are neither pro-Soviet nor eager to serve Western strategy, but deeply suspicious of Tripoli. Their leverage is armed kinship networks and control of eastern territory.

15.name: Bayt al-Shalhi
15.text:
The House of Shalhi is the family of Ibrahim al-Shalhi, King Idris's chamberlain, whose sons became the most powerful courtiers of the 1960s. Umar al-Shalhi, the king's adviser, escaped abroad when the monarchy fell and now works from Europe, while his brother, Colonel Abd al-Aziz al-Shalhi, is in detention.

Around the family gather contractors, agents of foreign oil companies and merchants who prospered from concessions, land deals and royal patronage. They want the return of a business-friendly monarchy, Western investment and the end of the officers' anti-corruption trials. Their leverage is money held abroad, foreign contacts and knowledge of the old regime's secrets.

16.name: Ghurfat Tijarat wa Sina'at Tarabulus
16.english: Tripoli Chamber of Commerce and Industry
16.text:
The Tripoli Chamber of Commerce and Industry represents the merchants, importers, shopkeepers and small manufacturers of the capital, many of whom have prospered from the oil boom of the 1960s. Since the revolution its members fear controls on trade, foreign exchange and the property of foreigners on whom much commerce depends.

The chamber stands for private enterprise, open markets, low taxes, protection of property and a predictable legal order. It favours commercial ties with Italy and the West but avoids open politics. Its leverage lies in the suq, import licences and the daily supply of goods to the cities, which the new regime cannot yet do without.

17.name: Hurras al-Jabal al-Akhdar
17.text:
The Guardians of the Green Mountain are foresters, agronomists and university teachers who warn that the juniper and cypress forests of the Jabal al-Akhdar are being cleared and overgrazed, and that the fossil water beneath the desert at Kufra is being pumped without regard for the future. They have no organization beyond professional circles in Bayda, Benghazi and Tripoli.

They call for reforestation, protection of the coastal aquifers against salt intrusion, careful use of oil revenues for sustainable agriculture and limits on uncontrolled urban growth. Indifferent to the Cold War, they seek influence through ministries of agriculture and planning, where their expertise is respected but rarely obeyed.

18.name: Harakat al-Qawmiyyin al-Arab
18.text:
The Arab Nationalist Movement, founded in Beirut by George Habash and his comrades, built a Libyan branch among students, teachers and officials in the 1960s and was repeatedly prosecuted under the monarchy. Since the September revolution some of its sympathizers serve the new regime, while the movement itself, split across the Arab world, cannot organize openly.

It stands for Arab unity, social justice, land reform, nationalization of foreign economic interests and support for the Palestinian fedayeen. It rejects Western bases and Israel and leans toward the socialist countries without accepting communist leadership. Its leverage is ideological closeness to the officers and a cadre of educated activists.

19.name: Al-Khatt al-Sini
19.text:
The Chinese Line is a handful of student and teacher reading circles in Benghazi and Tripoli that draw on Mao Zedong's writings, the Palestinian fedayeen's doctrine of people's war and the Marxist wing of the Arab nationalist movement. They have no party and avoid open activity under the new regime.

They condemn both American imperialism and Soviet revisionism, call for arming the people, agrarian revolution in the oases and a self-reliant economy, and see the officers' revolution as incomplete. Their leverage is minimal, but their slogans resonate among radicalized youth impatient with both the monarchy's legacy and the new officers' caution.

20.name: Hizb al-Mu'tamar al-Watani
20.text:
The National Congress Party was Bashir al-Sadawi's Tripolitanian nationalist party, which demanded a unitary independent Libya and opposed the federal monarchy. After the disputed 1952 election and riots it was banned and Sadawi deported; he died in exile in 1957, but his followers remain a recognizable milieu in Tripoli.

Its heirs champion a centralized Arab Libya, the end of Cyrenaican and royal privilege, the removal of foreign bases and a popular voice for the urban masses. Many welcome the revolution as vindication while resenting rule by young officers. Their leverage is a populist tradition in Tripoli and old networks among merchants and notables.

21.name: Quarta Sponda
21.text:
The Fourth Shore is named after Mussolini's term for colonial Libya. It is the nostalgic milieu among the roughly twenty thousand Italians still farming and trading in Tripolitania, descendants of the fascist-era settlers, some of whom keep contacts with the Italian Social Movement at home. Since the revolution they live in growing fear for their land and businesses.

They cling to the memory of Italian Libya, demand protection of their property and look to Rome and the Western alliance for guarantees. Hostile to Arab nationalism and to the officers, they have no prospect of power, but they control farms, workshops and capital that the new regime covets.

22.name: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Arabiyya al-Libiyya
22.text:
The Libyan Arab Armed Forces are the small regular army of some ten thousand men, trained by British missions and now enlarged with the absorbed security forces of the monarchy. The Free Officers rule in their name, but in December 1969 Defence Minister Adam al-Hawwaz and Interior Minister Musa Ahmad were arrested for plotting against the Revolutionary Command Council.

Senior officers outside the Free Officers' circle want professional autonomy, modern weapons, discipline and an end to political interference, and many quietly prefer collective military rule to one man's leadership. The army is the arbiter of Libyan politics; whoever commands its garrisons in Tripoli and Benghazi decides the regime's fate.

23.name: Al-Usra al-Sanusiyya
23.text:
The House of Senussi is the dynasty of the Senussi order that ruled independent Libya from 1951 until the coup of 1 September 1969. King Idris I was abroad for medical treatment when the officers struck and now lives in exile in Egypt, while Crown Prince Hasan al-Rida, forced to renounce his rights, is held under arrest in Libya.

Royalists seek the restoration of the constitutional monarchy of 1951, respect for Islam and tribal tradition, and the return of the alliance with Britain and the United States. Their support lies in Cyrenaica, among the Senussi brethren and the eastern tribes, and in exiles abroad willing to fund a countercoup.
